question: A METAR is:

options.text: A coded forecast for an aerodrome covering the next 9 to 30 hours
A coded warning of hazardous en-route weather for an FIR
A coded forecast of upper winds and temperatures by flight level
A coded report of the observed weather at an aerodrome at a stated time

explanation: METARs report actual conditions. Forecasts for aerodromes are TAFs; warnings for an FIR are SIGMETs.

question: METARs are usually issued:

options.text: Every 6 hours, at the main synoptic hours
Once a day, at the start of operations
Every 30 minutes, or hourly at some aerodromes
Only when the weather changes significantly

explanation: Routine reports are issued half-hourly or hourly. A SPECI is issued between routine reports when conditions change significantly.

question: In the METAR group "121150Z", the figures mean:

options.text: Valid from 12 to 11, 50 minutes
The 12th day of the month at 1150 UTC
12 November at 1150 local time, the time of issue
1211 UTC with a 50 kt wind

explanation: The date–time group gives the day of the month and the time of observation in UTC (Z).

question: The wind in a METAR is given as:

options.text: True direction to the nearest 10°, with the 10-minute mean speed
Magnetic direction, with the wind speed at 2000 ft
True direction to the nearest 5°, with the 2-minute mean speed
Magnetic direction to the nearest degree, with the peak gust

explanation: METAR winds are true and are 10-minute means. Winds passed by the tower for take-off and landing are magnetic.

question: The METAR wind group "24018G32KT" means:

options.text: 240° magnetic, 18 kt, varying by 32°
Wind from 240° at 32 kt, gusts of 18 kt
240° true, mean 18 kt, gusting to 32 kt
240° true, 18 kt, gusts expected in 32 minutes

explanation: G introduces the maximum gust. Gusts are only reported when they exceed the mean speed by 10 kt or more.

question: The METAR group "31008KT 280V350" means:

options.text: The wind is variable from 280° to 350° at 31 kt
The wind is 310° at 8 kt, veering to 350° and then backing to 280° later
Two runways, 28 and 35, are in use
The wind is 310° at 8 kt, with the direction varying between 280° and 350°

explanation: The variability group shows the extreme directions during the previous 10 minutes when the variation is significant.

question: Calm wind is coded in a METAR as:

options.text: VRB00KT
CALM

explanation: All zeros indicate calm. VRB is used for a light wind of variable direction, for example VRB02KT.

question: The visibility reported in the main visibility group of a METAR is:

options.text: The lowest visibility in any direction, whatever part of the horizon or aerodrome it covers
The prevailing visibility, reached or exceeded over at least half the horizon or aerodrome
The visibility measured from the cockpit of a landing aircraft
The RVR measured on the main runway in use

explanation: If visibility in one direction is markedly lower (below 1500 m, or less than half the prevailing value), the minimum and its direction are added.

question: In a METAR, a visibility of 10 km or more is coded as:

options.text: 10KM
P6SM

explanation: 9999 means 10 km or more. 0000 means less than 50 m.

question: The METAR visibility group "3000 1200NE" means:

options.text: Visibility varying between 1200 m and 3000 m in all directions
Visibility 3000 m, with an RVR of 1200 m on the north-east runway
Visibility 3000 m now, decreasing to 1200 m within the next hour
Prevailing 3000 m, with a minimum of 1200 m towards the north-east

explanation: The minimum visibility and its direction are reported when they differ significantly from the prevailing value.

question: RVR is included in a METAR when:

options.text: Visibility or RVR is less than 1500 m
Precipitation of any kind is falling
Visibility is less than 5000 m in any direction
The cloud base is lower than 1000 ft

explanation: RVR is the operational figure for low visibility and is reported whenever visibility or RVR falls below 1500 m.

question: The METAR group "R27/0650D" means:

options.text: Runway 27 is closed for the next 650 minutes
RVR on runway 27 is 650 m and has been decreasing
Visibility on runway 27 is 6500 m, decreasing
RVR on runway 27 is 65 m, with deep snow

explanation: U shows an upward tendency, D a downward tendency and N no distinct change over the previous 10 minutes.

question: In an RVR group, the letter P before the value (for example R09/P2000) means:

options.text: The runway is only partly contaminated
The RVR is above the highest value the system can assess
The RVR is below the lowest value the system can assess
The RVR is a forecast rather than an observed value

explanation: P (plus) shows the value is above the upper limit of the measuring system; M (minus) shows it is below the lower limit.

question: The METAR weather group "+SHRA" means:

options.text: Heavy showers of rain
Rain showers in the vicinity
Moderate rain with shallow fog
Light showers of rain

explanation: + means heavy, SH means showers and RA means rain. No sign would indicate moderate intensity.

question: The METAR weather group "-DZ" means:

options.text: Drizzle in the vicinity
Light dust
Light drizzle
Heavy drizzle

explanation: The minus sign indicates light intensity and DZ is drizzle.

question: In a METAR, "VCSH" means:

options.text: Very cold showers falling at the aerodrome
Visibility reduced by showers at the aerodrome
Showers containing volcanic ash nearby
Showers in the vicinity, but not at the aerodrome

explanation: VC (vicinity) indicates the phenomenon is within about 8 km of the aerodrome but not at it.

question: In a METAR, "BR" stands for:

options.text: Mist
Breaking cloud
Blowing snow
Haze

explanation: BR (from the French "brume") is mist: visibility of 1000 to 5000 m due to water droplets.

question: In a METAR, "HZ" stands for:

options.text: Hazardous weather
Mist
Haze
Hail

explanation: Haze is a reduction in visibility caused by dry particles such as dust or smoke.

question: In a METAR, "FZFG" means:

options.text: Fog mixed with smoke from industry
Shallow fog, less than 2 m deep
Fog in patches lying across the aerodrome
Freezing fog, with supercooled droplets

explanation: FZ (freezing) indicates supercooled liquid water that will freeze on contact.

question: In a METAR, "BCFG" means:

options.text: Blowing fog
Fog patches
Fog in the vicinity
Freezing fog

explanation: BC is the descriptor for patches. MIFG is shallow fog and PRFG partial fog.

question: In a METAR, "MIFG" means:

options.text: Moderate fog
Fog with mist
Fog patches
Shallow fog

explanation: MI (shallow) fog is a thin layer, often less than 2 m deep, which may leave the sky visible above.

question: In a METAR, "GR" and "GS" represent:

options.text: Gusts, and gale-force squalls
Graupel and glazed ice
Hail, and small hail or snow pellets
Ground fog, and ground snow lying on the runways

explanation: GR is hail (5 mm or more). GS is small hail (less than 5 mm) and/or snow pellets.

question: In a METAR, "TSRA" means:

options.text: A thunderstorm with no precipitation
A thunderstorm with moderate rain
A tropical storm with rain
Thunder and rain in the vicinity

explanation: TS on its own means a thunderstorm without precipitation at the station; the precipitation type is added when it occurs.

question: A thunderstorm is reported in a METAR when:

options.text: Thunder has been heard within the last 10 minutes
Lightning has been seen at any distance within the last hour
Hail has fallen at any time that day
Cumulonimbus is forecast

explanation: The present weather TS is used when thunder has been heard in the 10 minutes before the observation.

question: In a METAR, "VA" stands for:

options.text: Volcanic ash
Valley fog
Variable
Visibility above minimums

explanation: Volcanic ash is reported as an obscuration because of its effect on visibility and its serious hazard to engines.

question: In a METAR, "SQ" means:

options.text: Sandstorm
Small hail
Snow showers
Squall

explanation: SQ is a squall, a sudden increase in wind lasting a minute or more.

question: In a METAR, "FC" means:

options.text: Freezing cloud with supercooled water
Fog and cloud combined at the surface
Funnel cloud (tornado or waterspout)
Forecast change expected within 2 hours

explanation: FC indicates a funnel cloud; +FC is a well-developed tornado or waterspout.

question: In a METAR, "SS" and "DS" stand for:

options.text: Sea spray and dry snow
Sandstorm and duststorm
Snow showers and drifting snow
Small hail and dust

explanation: Both reduce visibility, often severely, in desert regions.

question: The METAR group "BLSN" means:

options.text: Blowing snow, raised to 2 m or more
Heavy snowfall from nimbostratus
Drifting snow, kept below 2 m
Snow showers from cumulus

explanation: BL (blowing) means raised by the wind to eye level or higher. DR (drifting) is used below 2 m.

question: In a METAR, "RERA" at the end of the report indicates:

options.text: Rain is expected to start at the aerodrome within the next hour
Heavy rain is falling at the time of observation
Moderate or heavy rain has recently stopped or weakened
The runway surface is still wet from earlier rain

explanation: The RE prefix marks recent weather of operational significance.

question: The METAR group "WS R27" indicates:

options.text: Warnings in force for runway 27
A wet surface on runway 27
The mean wind speed measured at the threshold of runway 27
Windshear has been reported on runway 27

explanation: Windshear information may be added to a METAR for one runway or for all runways (WS ALL RWY).

question: The METAR cloud group "BKN012" means:

options.text: 5–7 oktas, base 120 ft above aerodrome level
5–7 oktas, base 1200 ft above aerodrome level
1–2 oktas, base 1200 ft above aerodrome level
5–7 oktas, base 12 000 ft above aerodrome level

explanation: Cloud heights are in hundreds of feet above aerodrome level.

question: The METAR cloud group "SCT030CB" means:

options.text: Cumulonimbus covering the whole sky at 3000 ft
3–4 oktas of cloud at 300 ft, with a ceiling
3–4 oktas of cumulonimbus with a base of 3000 ft
Scattered showers with a base of 3000 ft

explanation: The only cloud types named in a METAR are CB and TCU.

question: In a METAR, which cloud types are identified by name?

options.text: Only stratus and nimbostratus, as low cloud
Only cirrus, as high cloud
All ten main cloud types, each abbreviated
Only cumulonimbus (CB) and towering cumulus (TCU)

explanation: Only the significant convective cloud types are named; other cloud is described only by amount and height.

question: In a METAR, "VV001" means:

options.text: Sky obscured, with a vertical visibility of 100 ft
Variable visibility of about 1 km
Cloud at 100 ft covering 1 okta
Horizontal visibility of 100 m in thick freezing fog

explanation: When the sky is obscured, for example by fog, the vertical visibility replaces the cloud group.

question: For CAVOK to be reported, the conditions include:

options.text: No cloud below 1500 ft above the aerodrome and no precipitation, whatever the visibility
10 km or more, no cloud below 5000 ft or the highest MSA (if greater), no CB or TCU, no significant weather
10 km or more and no cloud of any kind at any level, although light precipitation is allowed
5 km or more, no cloud below 3000 ft or the highest MSA (if lower), and no thunderstorms at the aerodrome

explanation: CAVOK replaces the visibility, RVR, weather and cloud groups when all four conditions are met.

question: Can CAVOK be reported when there is a layer of cloud at 8000 ft and the highest minimum sector altitude is 4500 ft, with visibility 20 km and no weather?

options.text: No, because the visibility must be exactly 10 km
Yes, as all the CAVOK conditions are met
No, because there is cloud present
Only if the cloud is cumulonimbus

explanation: Cloud above 5000 ft (and above the highest MSA) is allowed, provided it is not CB or TCU.

question: The abbreviation "NSC" in a METAR means:

options.text: No special conditions, so that no SPECI will be issued before the next METAR
Night sky clear, used only for reports made between sunset and sunrise
No snow cover on any of the runways, so that no runway state group needs to be included
No cloud below 5000 ft or the highest MSA and no CB or TCU, where CAVOK does not apply

explanation: NSC is used when there is no cloud of operational significance but CAVOK is not appropriate, for example because the visibility is below 10 km.

question: The METAR group "M04/M07" means:

options.text: Temperature −4°C, dew point −7°C
Temperature 4°C, dew point 7°C
Minimum temperature 4°C, maximum 7°C
Temperature −4°C, dew point +7°C

explanation: M stands for minus.

question: The METAR group "Q0998" means:

options.text: Pressure altitude 998 ft
QFF 998 hPa
QNH 998 hPa
QFE 998 hPa

explanation: The QNH is the only pressure given in a METAR, rounded down to a whole hectopascal, with a leading zero if below 1000.

question: If the actual QNH is 1012.8 hPa, the METAR will report:
explanation: QNH is always rounded down to the whole hectopascal below.

question: A TREND forecast attached to a METAR is valid for:

options.text: 9 hours
2 hours from the time of observation
1 hour from the time of issue of the METAR
24 hours

explanation: TRENDs give the expected changes in the next two hours using BECMG, TEMPO or NOSIG.

question: "NOSIG" at the end of a METAR means:

options.text: No signal received from the instruments
No significant weather is occurring at the time of the observation
No significant change expected in the next 2 hours
The report was not signed by the observer

explanation: NOSIG is a TREND indicating the conditions are expected to stay much the same.

question: In a METAR TREND, "TEMPO FM1400 TL1530 3000 SHRA" means:

options.text: Temporarily, between 1400 and 1530 UTC, 3000 m in moderate showers
At 1400 UTC visibility 3000 m, and at 1530 UTC showers
Showers within 3000 m of the aerodrome from 1400 to 1530 local time
From 1400 UTC, a permanent change to 3000 m in showers

explanation: TEMPO means temporary fluctuations, each lasting less than an hour and together less than half the period.

question: In a METAR TREND, "BECMG AT1800 9999 NSW" means:

options.text: Visibility 9999 m, becoming worse from 1800 UTC
No snow on the runway from 1800 UTC
From 1800 UTC, the visibility improves temporarily to 10 km
At 1800 UTC, visibility 10 km or more and the weather ends

explanation: NSW means no significant weather. BECMG with AT gives the time by which the change will be complete.

question: "AUTO" in a METAR indicates:

options.text: The report is a forecast, not an observation
The wind direction is varying automatically through 360°
Generated by an automatic station without human intervention
The aerodrome is closed to traffic

explanation: Elements the automatic system cannot determine are replaced by slashes rather than omitted.

question: In an AUTO METAR, "////" in place of the visibility means:

options.text: The visibility could not be determined by the system
The visibility is less than 50 m in thick fog
The runway is closed
The visibility is 10 km or more

explanation: Slashes replace each element that cannot be measured.

question: A SPECI is:

options.text: A report of volcanic ash only, issued by a volcanic ash advisory centre
A special report between routine METARs when conditions change significantly
A forecast of special weather phenomena for the whole flight information region
A report issued once a day summarising the weather of the previous 24 hours

explanation: It has the same format as a METAR with SPECI replacing METAR.

question: In a METAR runway state group, the code "R88" refers to:

options.text: Runway 08 and 26
The runway with the lowest friction
A repeat of the previous report
All runways

explanation: R99 is a repetition of the last report because no new information has been received.

question: "SNOCLO" in a METAR means:

options.text: Snow showers at the aerodrome have ended
Snow-bearing clouds are present over the aerodrome
The aerodrome is closed because of runway contamination
Snow clearance of the runways is complete

explanation: SNOCLO replaces the runway state group when the aerodrome is closed due to deposits on the runways.

question: Decode: METAR LFPG 041130Z 19014KT 160V230 6000 -RA BKN008 OVC020 11/10 Q1004 NOSIG. The ceiling is:

options.text: 800 ft, the base of the broken layer
600 ft
2000 ft, the base of the overcast layer

explanation: The ceiling is the lowest layer of 5 oktas or more (BKN or OVC), here BKN008.

question: Decode: METAR EGLL 151020Z 05006KT 0300 R27R/0450N FG VV002 03/03 Q1028. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Mist, 3 km; RVR 27R 450 m, no change; cloud base 200 ft
Fog, 300 m; RVR 27R 450 m, no change; vertical visibility 200 ft
Freezing fog, 300 m; RVR 27R 450 m; cloud base 2000 ft
Fog, 300 ft; RVR 27R 4500 m, increasing; vertical visibility 2000 ft

explanation: FG with 300 m visibility; the RVR group shows 450 m with N (no distinct tendency); VV002 is a vertical visibility of 200 ft.

question: Decode: METAR LIRF 201450Z 27015G28KT 9999 VCTS FEW035CB SCT040 24/16 Q1012 RETSRA. Which is correct?

options.text: Thunderstorm with rain now at the aerodrome, visibility 9 km or more, wind 270/15 steady
No cumulonimbus present, wind variable, recent rain without thunder
Thunderstorm in the vicinity, recent thunderstorm with rain, wind 270/15 gusting 28
Volcanic ash in the vicinity, wind 270/15 gusting 28, no recent weather

explanation: VCTS means a thunderstorm within about 8 km but not at the aerodrome; RETSRA shows that a thunderstorm with rain affected the aerodrome recently.

question: In a METAR, "VRB04KT" means:

options.text: A wind varying between calm and 4 kt
A light 4 kt wind whose direction is variable
Calm conditions, with gusts of 4 kt
A 4 kt wind veering steadily through the period

explanation: VRB is used when the direction cannot be given as a mean, usually because the wind is light.

question: In a METAR, "0000" in the visibility group means:

options.text: Visibility 10 km or more
Visibility not observed
Visibility exactly 0 m because the aerodrome is closed
Visibility less than 50 m

explanation: 0000 is the lowest code value, meaning below 50 m.

question: In a METAR, "-SN BLSN" means:

options.text: Light snow falling, with snow also blown to 2 m or more
Light snow falling, with snow drifting below 2 m only
Heavy snow falling in the vicinity of the aerodrome
Light sleet falling, with snow on the ground

explanation: Several weather groups may be reported together. BL indicates snow raised by the wind to eye level or higher.

question: In a METAR, "RASN" means:

options.text: Rain with snow lying on the ground
Snow in the vicinity of rain showers
Rain and snow mixed (sleet)
Rain followed by snow later

explanation: Two precipitation types can be combined in one group, with the dominant type first.

question: In a METAR, "FZDZ" means:

options.text: Drizzle that has recently stopped
Freezing drizzle, which freezes on contact
Drizzle that has frozen into ice pellets
Drizzle together with fog at the aerodrome

explanation: FZ shows supercooled drops that will form clear ice on impact.

question: In a METAR, "PRFG" means:

options.text: Fog in the vicinity of the aerodrome, but not at the aerodrome itself
Fog patches randomly scattered over the aerodrome
Freezing fog with supercooled droplets
Partial fog covering a substantial part of the aerodrome

explanation: PR (partial) means part of the aerodrome is covered by fog while the rest is clear.

question: In a METAR, "FU" stands for:

options.text: Smoke
Freezing
Fog with ultraviolet
Funnel cloud

explanation: FU (from the French "fumée") is smoke.

question: In a METAR, "TCU" means:

options.text: Turbulence in cumulus
Towering cumulus
Thunderstorm in cumulus
Tropical cyclone

explanation: TCU is cumulus congestus, reported along with CB because of its operational significance.

question: Decode: "METAR LEMD 271500Z 36004KT 320V040 CAVOK 34/06 Q1014 NOSIG". Which statement is correct?

options.text: 360/40, visibility 3200 m, temperature 34°C, dew point 6°C, QNH 1014
Variable wind, CAVOK, temperature 6°C, dew point 34°C, QNH 1014
360/04 varying 320–040, CAVOK, temperature 34°C, dew point 6°C, QNH 1014
Calm, cloud at 4000 ft, temperature 34°C, dew point 6°C, QNH 1014

explanation: The large dew-point spread shows very dry air; CAVOK means no cloud below 5000 ft or MSA and visibility 10 km or more.

question: Decode: "METAR EHAM 090825Z 22024G38KT 4500 SHRA BKN014CB OVC025 08/06 Q0987 TEMPO 1500 +TSRA". The TREND indicates:

options.text: Thunderstorms with heavy rain already occurring at the time of observation
A 15% chance of thunderstorms with heavy rain in the next 2 hours
A permanent change to 1500 m from the time of observation at 0825
Temporary spells within 2 hours of 1500 m in thunderstorms with heavy rain

explanation: TEMPO in a METAR TREND means temporary fluctuations expected within the next two hours.

question: Decode: "METAR UUEE 120600Z 00000KT 0150 R24/0300V0500 FZFG VV001 M08/M09 Q1031". Which statement is correct?

options.text: Calm, 150 m in freezing fog, RVR 24 varying 300–500 m, vertical visibility 100 ft
Calm, 150 m in snow, temperature −8°C, cloud base 1000 ft
Wind 240° at 30 kt, 150 m in freezing fog, vertical visibility 100 ft
Calm, 1500 m in mist, RVR on runway 24 of 300 m, cloud base 100 ft

explanation: Variable RVR is shown as a range with V between the two values.

question: In a METAR, a cloud group "FEW008///" from an automatic station indicates:

options.text: Few clouds at 8000 ft, of three different types not identified
Sky obscured, vertical visibility 800 ft
Cloud amount not measured, base 800 ft
Few clouds at 800 ft, type not determined by the system

explanation: Automatic systems cannot always identify CB or TCU, so the type is replaced by slashes.

question: An automatic METAR reports "NCD". This means:

options.text: No change detected since the last report
Nil cloud data, as the sensor has failed
No cloud detected by the automatic system
No ceiling, but CB present nearby

explanation: NCD is used by automatic systems when no cloud is detected; it does not exclude cloud the sensor cannot see.
